newsitem.title: USA: Republicans offer to work with Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Republicans offer to work with Clinton.

text.p: U.S. Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott promised on Saturday to cooperate with President Bill Clinton if he was sincere about wanting to balance the budget and reduce government.
Republicans kept control of the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections while Clinton won a second term.
Lott, in a response to Clinton's weekly radio address, said Republicans wanted to put the bitterness of the campaign behind them and work together for the good of the country.
"And if President Clinton meant what he said during the campaign, that cooperation will be forthcoming," Lott, of Mississippi, said.

"He said the era of big government is over and admitted the need for lower taxes and less regulation. He talked tough about crime and accepted major Republican legislation on welfare and illegal immigration.
"If he sincerely wants to follow through on all that -- helping the Congress deal with the nation's most pressing problems -- then we can do it together.

"But if not -- if he reverts to his old agenda of expanding government -- if he names the kind of federal judges who would overturn this week's election results with next year's court decisions -- and, if his 'bridge to the future' turns out to be a toll bridge for the taxpayers, then we will resist with every fiber of our being," Lott said.

Separately Deputy Senate Republican Leader Don Nickles of Oklahoma also promised to work with Clinton if possible. But he warned Clinton might be impeached if he pardoned anyone in the Whitewater investigation or tried to fire Independent Counsel Ken Starr.

Nickles, on Cable News Network's "Evans and Novak" programme, compared the situation to the Watergate scandal that ended with the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974 before he could be impeached.
Nickles also said Hillary Rodham Clinton might be indicted over the 1993 firing of seven White House Travel Office employees. She has denied any role in their dismissals.
"I think there's some real problems there facing the first lady concerning possible obstruction of justice, and/or perjury. I wouldn't be surprised if she's indicted." he said.

Clinton, in his broadcast, said he wanted Republicans to join him in balancing the budget in a way that strengthens families. He also called the decision of the U.S. liquor industry decision to end its voluntary ban on television and radio advertising "irresponsible."
Lott said the message of the election was that voters wanted a smaller, more efficient government that operates on a balanced budget and does not tolerate corruption.
"That's what congressional Republicans will keep working for. On behalf of all my colleagues, I invite President Clinton to join us in that effort," he said.
Clinton will meet congressional leaders next Tuesday to discuss the budget and other issues they will face in the next session of Congress that begins on Jan. 7.
Lott said on Wednesday that Republicans would press early next year for passage of a constiutional amendment to require a balanced federal budget. Republicans also want a tax cut.
